name: OMAN

flag.title: Flag of Oman
flag.note: Red, white & green with khanjar dagger

lead: Oman is at the tip of Arabia, where desert mountains tumble into the sea. People have traded frankincense, a perfumed tree resin, here for 5,000 years. White forts, turquoise pools and a 3,000 km coast make it an adventure.
geo: Oman is mostly desert and rocky mountains. Wadis, which are dry riverbeds, fill with turquoise pools after rain. Jebel Shams sometimes gets frost.
In the south, the Dhofar cliffs turn bright green each summer when monsoon mist rolls in. The coast stretches over 3,000 km.
animals: Up to 20,000 green turtle mothers lay eggs on the beach at Ras al Jinz each year. Arabian oryx, a desert antelope, died out in the wild, but Oman bred them.
Whale sharks glide offshore and spinner dolphins surf the waves. In the mountains, rare Arabian leopards pad silently over ancient rocks.
culture: Guests get qahwa (spiced coffee) and sticky dates. On special occasions, men wear a white dishdasha robe and a curved khanjar dagger. The khanjar is on the flag.
Salalah, a southern city, is the frankincense capital. Workers tap milky sap from Boswellia trees and burn it as incense (sweet smoke). Omani music has African rhythms from centuries of trade.
history: Omani sailors built a trading empire from East Africa to China. The explorer Marco Polo called the city of Qalhat one of the finest ports in the world.
Portugal seized Omani ports in the 1500s but was driven out. Oman controlled the island of Zanzibar by the 18th century. In 1970, Sultan Qaboos began to modernise a country with just three schools.
wows: Oman has burned frankincense for over 5,000 years.
The 3,000-year-old falaj water system still feeds farms through over 1,000 km of tunnels.
The Wahiba Sands desert has dunes as tall as a 25-storey building.
Oryx were declared extinct in the wild in 1972, then Oman saved them.
Muttrah souq (market) has traded nonstop for 200 years and smells of oud (perfume wood).
Oman has over 1,000 forts and castles, more for its size than almost anywhere.
Green turtles return, decades later, to the very beach where they were born.

myths.myth: Camels store water in their humps
myths.fact: Humps hold fat, not water. The fat gives energy when food is scarce.
Wind slowly pushes dunes along. Some creep several metres every year.
